# Grundlage

Zero-dependency library for building web components with tagged template literals.
Server-rendered and hydrated on the client. `npm install grundlage`.

## Mental model

A component is a generator function passed to `component`. It runs ONCE when the element
mounts and runs to completion (never `while (true)`): setup code runs, then something
renderable is yielded (a render function, an `html` template, or an inner generator). The
generator's ONE argument is a props object carrying `host` plus every prop declared in
`component(gen, { props })`; a `yield` of a renderable evaluates back to the host element.
A returned function is the cleanup. There are no signals and no hooks. A re-render happens
on `host.update()`, on `host.setProp(…)`, on assigning a declared prop to a NEW value, and
when a DECLARED attribute on the host element changes. An undeclared attribute (`class`,
`style`, `data-*`) does not re-render. State declared before the `yield` survives updates because the yielded
render function closes over it; the generator body itself does not re-run.

## Complete example

```javascript
import { component, html } from "grundlage";

// the schema is a plain object; hoisting it keeps the element's inputs readable at a glance
const props = { start: [Number, 0], label: [String, "count"] };

customElements.define(
	"click-counter",
	component(
		function* ({ host, start }) {
			let count = start; // `start` is a SEED: the generator body runs once

			const increment = () => {
				count += 1;
				host.update(); // re-calls the yielded render function below; count is still here
			};

			// destructured in the render function, so `label` is LIVE, re-read every update
			yield ({ label }) =>
				html`<button onClick=${increment}>${label}: ${count}</button>`;
		},
		{ props },
	),
);
```

## API

`component(generator, options?) => CustomElementConstructor`
  Register the return value with `customElements.define`. The first argument MUST be a
  generator function (`function*` or `async function*`). A plain or arrow function throws
  a `TypeError` at definition time, not at mount. `options` extends `ShadowRootInit`; the
  defaults are `{ mode: "open", clonable: true, delegatesFocus: true, serializable: true }`
  and any option passed overrides its default. `options.props` is the SCHEMA (see below):
  it fixes the observed attributes and installs one accessor per prop on the element class.
  `formAssociated: true` swaps the base class for the form-associated one. `{ mode: "closed" }`
  still hydrates and replays `load` data: the closed root is reached through
  `attachInternals().shadowRoot` instead of `host.shadowRoot`, so server output is reused
  rather than re-rendered. The return value is a class. `class extends component(fn) {}` is
  the extension point for methods, getters and static fields; nothing is assigned to `host`
  at runtime.

`options.props`, the schema
  `{ propName: entry }`, where an entry is a FUNCTION taking whatever arrived and returning
  the value, or `undefined` to REFUSE it: `(incoming) => incoming instanceof Quote ?
  incoming : undefined`. `String`, `Number`, `BigInt` and `Boolean` are shorthands for the
  four shipped functions. `[entry, fallback]` supplies what the function is called with when
  nothing was supplied. That is the whole schema. There is no separate optional or required
  shape, and no type guard: a prop is its function.

  The function is the ONE place a value is parsed or validated, and it serves both channels.
  A string means the value came from markup and needs parsing; anything else came from JS and
  is already itself: `(incoming) => typeof incoming === "string" ? incoming.split(" ") :
  incoming`.

  Five rules cover the whole model:

  1. ONE VALUE PER PROP, in one store the element owns. Last write wins, whichever channel it
     came from, and nothing is compared across channels.
  2. EVERY INCOMING VALUE runs through the prop's function: markup, a property assignment, a
     parent's binding, `setProp`, the fallback at construction.
  3. A REFUSAL IS IGNORED. The previous value stays and the console warns; nothing throws and
     nothing re-renders.
  4. ABSENCE IS A WRITE OF THE FALLBACK. `removeAttribute`, `el.x = undefined`, `el.x = null`
     and element construction are one code path, so NOTHING is required and no read fails.
     The fallback is not restored: the function is asked the same question and gives the same
     answer, whenever it is asked.
  5. A PROPERTY ASSIGNMENT REFLECTS when the value it settled on has a string spelling. An
     attribute arriving from markup does not: `count="007"` stays as written while `el.count`
     reads `7`.

  Every prop observes an attribute: the LOWERCASED prop name. `userId` observes `userid`,
  and either spelling binds in markup. Prop names must match `/^[a-z][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*$/` and
  two props differing only in case throw at define time. Every declared prop becomes an
  accessor on the element class, so a name already on the prototype chain (`title`, `id`,
  `lang`, `hidden`, `update`, `setProp`, `internals`) throws at define time, as does `host`,
  which the props object reserves, and any name starting with `on-`, which markup reads as a
  custom event binding.

  A fallback is COPIED per element with `structuredClone` for anything object-shaped (deeply:
  a nested object is a fresh one too), and SHARED for a primitive, a function and a
  `Template`. A value `structuredClone` cannot reproduce (a class instance, an object
  holding a function) throws at define time and names the remedy: put the default inside the
  function, `(incoming) => incoming ?? new Value()`, which runs once per element. So does a
  fallback the prop's own function refuses; the check calls the function once, before any
  element exists.

  Reflection writes the value's own spelling: a string as itself, a number or bigint through
  `String(value)`, `true` as `""`. A value with no spelling (an object, `undefined`) takes a
  stale attribute OFF and touches nothing when there was none. `false` removes the attribute
  too, unless absence for that prop reads `true` (`[Boolean, true]`), where removing would
  say the opposite and it writes `"false"` instead. Reading is symmetric: `x`, `x=""` and
  `x="true"` are `true`, `x="false"` is `false`.

  The type layer sees the shape, not the function: a bare entry is `T | undefined`, and a
  `[entry, fallback]` is `T`. The visible fallback is the only way to promise a value. A
  bare `Boolean` is the exception, typed `boolean`, since absence is one of its two states.
  The fallback ITSELF is not type-checked against the entry: a wrong one is a define-time
  throw with a readable message rather than a compile error.

`` html`...` `` => `Template` (opaque)
  Tagged template literal. Each distinct literal is parsed once and cached (keyed by its
  strings array); later renders only touch dynamic parts. Yield it, or embed it inside
  another `html` template.

`props(element, schema) => typed object`
  The same schema, read once from a plain `HTMLElement` that never went through `component`,
  or for reading something deliberately left unobserved. NOT the primary spelling: a
  component declares its props in `component(gen, { props })` and receives them as its one
  argument. The returned object is a SNAPSHOT, and each call re-normalizes the schema. An own
  property under the prop name wins over the attribute (case intact: `element.userTags`, not
  `usertags`); with neither, the prop's function answers absence. A value the function refuses
  warns and reads as absent, the same as everywhere else. The export collides with the
  conventional `const props = {…}` schema name, so a module using both renames one
  (`import { props as readProps }`).

`load(host, fetcher, options?) => Promise<Value>`
  Data needed before the first render. On the server the fetcher runs and the result is
  serialized into the markup as a `<script type="application/json" data-ssr>`; on the client
  that payload is replayed once during hydration (the script is consumed) and every later
  call runs the fetcher normally. `options` is `{ key?, skipSsr? }`, or a string shorthand
  for `{ key }`. `skipSsr` skips the serialization only. The fetcher still runs on the
  server, and the client always fetches. Unkeyed replay is POSITIONAL (first payload to
  first `load`), so a conditional or reordered `load` can claim the wrong payload; a key
  pins each payload to its call, and unclaimed payloads warn on hydration.

`host.update() => Promise<void>`
  The re-render trigger. See Rules for what it re-fires and when it resolves. On the server
  it is always a no-op: the single server paint ends the run.

`host.setProp(name, value, oldValue?) => void`
  Imperative counterpart to a markup binding, for a framework/interop driver feeding props
  from outside. A DECLARED name is assigned through its own accessor, so it runs the prop's
  function, reflects and schedules, and `null`/`undefined` is the absence that writes the
  fallback back. An undeclared name resolves the same way a dynamic attribute does:
  stringable → attribute, non-stringable → property, `on*`/`on-*` plus a function → event
  listener. Pass `oldValue` so a previously bound listener is removed; the other channel is
  cleared either way.

`host.internals => ElementInternals | null`
  Lazily attached on first read, on every component, not only form-associated ones. `null`
  on the server.

Types: `BaseComponent`, `ComponentOptions`, `ComponentProps`, `LoadOptions`, `Resolve`,
`Schema`, `Template`.

## Bindings

```
content        <p>${text}</p>
attribute      <div class=${className}>
mixed attr     <div class="static ${dynamic}">
event          <button onClick=${handler}>          // on + EventName
custom event   <color-swatch on-swatch-select=${handler}>
spread         <div ${attributes}>                  // object → name/value, array → boolean attrs
list           <ul>${items.map((i) => html`<li>${i}</li>`)}</ul>
list key       <li><!--${item.id}-->…</li>          // first dynamic comment = row identity
nested         <div>${show && html`<details>…</details>`}</div>
dynamic tag    <${tagName}>content</${tagName}>
raw            <style>${css}</style>                // style/script/textarea
comment        <!-- note ${value} -->               // second and later dynamic comments
```

## Host attributes

If the OUTERMOST node of a render output is a `<template>` and it has no top-level siblings,
the wrapper is unwrapped: its children become the shadow DOM and its attributes are applied
to the host element. This is how a component sets its own `class`/`id`/`role`/handlers from
the inside.

```javascript
yield () => html`<template class="card" role="${role}" on-form-reset=${reset}>…</template>`;
```

- Static, dynamic, boolean, multi-part attributes and spreads all work and update between
  renders.
- Event handlers bind here too (e.g. `on-form-*` for form components).
- Attributes dropped by a later render are reverted on the host.
- A `<template>` WITH attributes in a nested position (content hole, list row) throws. A
  `<template>` that has top-level siblings is parsed as an ordinary element instead.

## Lists and keys

An array in a content hole renders one row per entry. Rows are matched by the row template's
identity and a content hash, which covers most reorders and edits without extra work. For
explicit identity, put a dynamic comment in the row: the FIRST dynamic comment of a template
is consumed as its key, never reaches the DOM, and binds that row's DOM (focus, scroll,
input state) to the value. Text around the expression is fine, it is constant across the
rows of one template, so only the expression tells rows apart: `<!--${id}-->` and
`<!-- key: ${id} -->` work the same way.

Row values: string / number / bigint render as text (`""`, `0`, `NaN` included); `null`,
`undefined`, `true`, `false` render nothing but still occupy a row; a nested array renders
recursively; anything else (plain object, `Date`, function, symbol) throws.

## Rules (get these right)

- The generator runs ONCE per mount and runs to completion, no `while (true)`. State
  declared before the `yield` persists across re-renders (the yielded render function closes
  over it), so mutable state belongs there rather than being re-derived.
- Don't hang state or methods on `host` (`host.query = …`, `host.close = () => …`). The host
  is not an instance bag. Keep state in generator-local variables, communicate outward by
  dispatching events and inward by reading attributes/props. Real methods come from extending
  the returned class (`class extends component(fn) {}`); a property assigned at runtime only
  exists once `connectedCallback` has run.
- Re-renders are triggered by `host.update()`, by `host.setProp(…)`, by assigning a declared
  prop a value it did not already hold (`el.items = […]`, `el.label = "x"`), and by a change
  to a DECLARED attribute. A write the prop's function refuses, and a re-write of the same
  primitive, schedule nothing. Undeclared attributes are not observed at all. There is no
  other reactivity.
- `update()` re-fires whatever was yielded LAST: a render function is re-called, an inner
  generator is torn down (its cleanup runs) and re-run from the top, and an `html` template
  yielded plainly from the component body never re-renders. After that yield `update()` is
  a no-op, as it is until the body reaches its FIRST renderable. The boundary is that yield,
  not the paint: an `update()` while a first async render is still pending DOES re-call the
  render function. The generator body itself never re-runs. A render
  function that returns a generator function is re-called too, and the branch it picks is torn
  down and re-installed. A component body that yields an inner generator and THEN paints its
  own content takes the shadow root back for good: the abandoned body is torn down at that
  paint, its pending async work can no longer land, and `update()` will not bring it back.
- `await host.update()` resolves once the DOM has been patched, in a microtask, not after
  the browser paints, there is no rAF in the path. For an async inner generator it resolves
  only when that generator's whole run completes, so the awaited state is the settled UI.
  Concurrent `update()` calls coalesce onto the pending pass and share its promise.
- A `yield` of a renderable (`html` template, render function, inner generator) evaluates to
  the host element: ``const host = yield () => html`…` ``. A yielded promise evaluates to its
  resolved value (`const data = yield fetch(...)`); any other value is echoed back. Render
  functions and inner generators receive the same props object the component body did.
- A yielded FUNCTION is always a render function: the yield position decides that, not what
  the function returns. Whatever it returns is committed as CONTENT, under the same rules as a
  content hole below: a template renders, `null`/`undefined`/`true`/`false` render nothing,
  strings/numbers/bigints render as text, an array renders as a list, and an object, a `Date`,
  a plain function or a symbol THROWS. So `` () => isOpen && html`…` `` clears the UI when
  `isOpen` goes false, and `` () => items.map(…) `` renders a list. The same values mean the
  same things at the root as they do in `${…}`. Returning nothing renders nothing and warns on
  the console: an arrow function with a block body needs an explicit `return`.
- Two return values escape the content rules. A render function may return a GENERATOR
  FUNCTION to choose which BODY runs (`` () => (isEditing ? editorBody : readOnlyBody) ``),
  and each branch is a full component body with its own setup, `yield` and cleanup, sharing the
  one shadow root. Switching branches runs the old branch's cleanup BEFORE the new branch's
  setup. Staying on the same branch still tears it down and re-runs it on every `update()`, so
  state that must survive belongs in the component body, not the branch. Returning content
  instead (`` () => (isOpen ? panelBody : null) ``) ends the branch: it is torn down as the
  content paints, so a `null` branch really is empty, not a body left running behind blank
  output. Missing the `*` is the mistake to watch for: a plain function is not a body and
  throws with that remedy.
- A render function may also return a PROMISE, on the client and on the server: the resolved
  value re-enters the same rulebook, so `` async () => html`…` `` renders once it settles and
  `` async () => someBody `` installs that body. Nothing is painted while it is pending, and
  `update()` re-calls the render function rather than waiting: the superseded call's result is
  discarded when it settles, however late, so the newest call always wins. A REJECTED render
  promise from a superseded call is discarded with it; a rejection from the current call is
  FATAL and is NOT thrown into the generator that yielded the render function, so a `try/catch`
  around that `yield` will not see it, so catch inside the render function. An INNER
  generator's render function is the one exception in reach: its rejection ends that inner
  generator, so the outer's `try/catch` around `yield innerBody` does see it.
- An inner generator may not introduce another generator function: one level of nesting only,
  whether it yields one or returns one from its render function; the attempt throws into the
  parent. So a delegated body may not delegate again.
- A returned function is the cleanup: it runs on disconnect, before an inner generator is
  re-run, and when the component body paints content over a running inner generator.
  `disconnectedCallback` waits a microtask and re-checks `isConnected`, so moving an element
  inside the DOM does NOT tear the component down.
- An uncaught error replaces the whole shadow tree with the error text and warns on the
  console. An error from an inner generator is thrown INTO the outer generator at its
  `yield`, so a `try/catch` there handles it; otherwise it reaches that root handler.
- In a CONTENT hole `null`, `undefined`, `false` and `true` render nothing, since a boolean is a
  condition result, not a value. Numbers, bigints and strings always render, `0`, `0n`,
  `NaN` and `""` included. So ``${isOpen && html`…`}`` is safe, but ``${items.length &&
  html`…`}`` writes the text `"0"` on an empty list; use a ternary for any non-boolean guard.
  An object, a function, a `Date` or a symbol in a content hole THROWS.
- In an ATTRIBUTE hole on an UNDECLARED name, `false`, `null` and `undefined` REMOVE the
  attribute and `true` sets it to `"true"`; a non-stringable value (object, array, function)
  is assigned as a PROPERTY instead, which is how data reaches a nested custom element.
  A name the target element DECLARES skips all of that and is assigned through that prop's
  accessor, whatever the value: `null` and `undefined` are the absence that writes the child's
  fallback back, and a value the child's function refuses warns from the PARENT's render frame
  and leaves the child's previous value standing. Where the child's definition has not loaded
  yet, nothing knows the name is declared: a stringable value rides the attribute the prop
  observes, anything else lands as an own property, and both reach the store at upgrade.
- Events bind as `onEventName=${handler}`. The name is matched case-insensitively against the
  element's own `on*` properties, so `onClick` and `onclick` both bind `click`; a name with no
  matching property is assigned as a dead property and warns on the console. A name the target
  DECLARES is a prop first and is never matched as an event, so `once: String` is settable,
  while `on-*` is refused at define time because markup has already claimed it. Custom events
  need the `on-` prefix (`on-swatch-select=${handler}`) and keep their hyphenated name
  verbatim. A quoted string (`onclick="…"`) is never a binding.
- Components render into SHADOW DOM by default. Light-DOM selectors won't reach inside.
- Don't write literal `<!--^.^ …-->` or `<!--*.*-->` comments in template HTML: those
  prefixes are the internal markers and a collision silently misaligns hydration.
- Change detection is HASH-BASED for strings, numbers, bigints, booleans, plain objects,
  arrays, `Map`, `Set` and nested templates: mutate-then-`update()` is detected (object
  graphs are walked to a depth of 64). Class instances, `Date`, typed arrays and functions
  are compared by REFERENCE identity, so mutating one in place reads as unchanged and is
  skipped. Pass plain data, or replace the reference to signal a change. A declared prop is
  the one place that does not skip: `el.items.push(x)` alone does not re-render, but
  `el.items = el.items` does, because a value that could have been mutated behind its
  reference is never called unchanged.
  It lands on the next render from any cause, where these hashes pick the new contents up.
- A dynamic `<style>` is fast when every `${…}` sits in a declaration VALUE: the mounted (and
  server-rendered) sheet text carries the real literal values, and every later update is a
  `setProperty` on this element's OWN CSSOM sheet, never a reparse, never a write to the
  host. Each instance owns a private sheet, so duplicates never collide. Structural holes
  (selector, property name, at-rule prelude), the same holed property declared twice in one
  block, an ambiguous `!important`, and a sheet the browser parses differently than the
  library expects (e.g. it drops a rule it can't parse) fall back to a full text rewrite that is
  always correct, just slower. Consequences: a runtime value the browser rejects (including
  one that smuggles `;` or `!important`) is dropped and the PREVIOUS value stays, a static
  `!important` is preserved as CSSOM priority, a CSS-wide keyword
  (`inherit`/`initial`/`unset`/`revert`) takes its normal effect, and serialized output
  (`getHTML`) reflects the last full-text write, not later CSSOM updates.
- Declare inputs in `component(gen, { props })` and read them off the object the generator
  and render functions receive. Don't read attributes directly: they're strings, they skip
  the parsing, defaults and refusal the schema gives, and an undeclared attribute does not
  re-render.
- The props object IS the store, so it is live rather than a snapshot: a value read after an
  `await` is current rather than the one the render started with. WHERE YOU DESTRUCTURE
  therefore decides what you get, and this is the most common mistake. The generator body
  runs ONCE, so `function* ({ label })` freezes `label` at mount. That is right for an initial
  value or a mount-time branch, WRONG for anything a render function paints. The render
  function runs per update, so `` yield ({ label }) => html`…` `` is live, and so is reading
  `componentProps.label` off the object. `{ ...componentProps }` is how you take a
  deliberate snapshot, by the language's own rule. The object is handed out READONLY: writing
  to it would move a value nothing parsed, reflected or scheduled on.
  `componentProps.host.count = 5` is the spelling that does all three, and it is the same one
  an outside caller uses (`element.count = 5`).
- `load` replays SSR data on hydration; don't add a fetch-once cache around it.
- Form components: `component(gen, { formAssociated: true })` re-dispatches the four form
  callbacks as host events `form-associated` `{form}`, `form-disabled` `{disabled}`,
  `form-reset` (no detail) and `form-state-restore` `{state, mode}`, bindable declaratively
  as `on-form-*` on the host `<template>`.
